note: English subtitle adaptation of the Chinese spoken text. Review against each cue before final render; only the Chinese text is sent to EdgeTTS.

captions.V3-01: In this paused game, we read Robert's available wars and estimated power against two targets; we did not declare war for him. His own estimate is 37,860 in both queries, but one effective defender exceeds 100,000 and the other is about 13,000. The first original target even resolves to another defender. What will the ruler choose from these different situations?
captions.V3-02: We will follow a war from the ruler's choice, through army objectives, approach and requests for help, to battle score and peace. The opening figures are real native readbacks; later numerical examples will be labelled as examples. In CK3 1.19.0.6, keep asking what is being compared, which condition lets the process continue, and what changes afterward.
captions.V3-03: An available Declare War button answers which wars a player can propose right now. The AI's own decision also considers whether to attack, which target and cause to use, power, restrictions, costs, scores and final selection. Robert's nine legal entries are not a record of that entire AI decision. An available button does not mean the AI has decided to fight.
captions.V3-04: Prewar money raises two questions: whether the ruler has set aside the required war reserves, and whether a particular declaration can be paid for. In the traced ordinary periodic path, gold and treasury war reserves each have their own requirement. A specific candidate then faces the cause's cost and the general interaction cost. Visible cash alone settles none of those separate checks.
captions.V3-05: The soldier count beside an army flag is not the strategic power estimate. Levies, men-at-arms, mercenaries, special troops and knights enter that estimate under different rules, and current and maximum-side estimates differ. A label containing 'maximum' does not mean every troop type is fully replenished: this path uses current composition for special troops. Do not translate strategic power into a headcount.
captions.V3-06: In Robert's first query, the effective defender is a different person from the original target; the second target stays the same. Robert's power is unchanged, while opposing power is 107,180 and 13,340. The native ratios, opposing power divided by Robert's power, are about 2.83 and 0.35. Identify the effective defender before interpreting an apparent choice of opponent.
captions.V3-07: The native relationship network looks for potential help through marriage, alliances and obligations to join, then checks potential call eligibility. Filtering differs between the two sides, so ally lists are not simply added together. Both network increments in Robert's readbacks are zero; that does not establish that these rulers have no allies. A relationship, an estimate, an accepted call and an arriving army are different outcomes.
captions.V3-08: Whether a target is already at war changes the military-power gate. In a simplified rule example without extra war or boldness modifiers, the permitted opposing-to-own ratio starts at 1.0 for a peaceful target and 1.5 for one already fighting. A ratio of 1.2 fails the first gate but passes the second. This widens consideration, without proving victory or skipping later cost, scoring and selection checks.
captions.V3-09: Suppose six positive-scoring candidates have scores of 100, 97, 94, 91, 90 and 89. The native filter draws a line at 90 percent of the highest score: 89 leaves and 90 remains. Exactly five remain, so no further top-five truncation is needed. The best card has an advantage, but every retained card is still eligible for the final draw.
captions.V3-10: The final draw uses the retained scores as weights. In this example their total is 472, so the 94-point card has 94 of those shares, roughly one fifth. Random choice happens among filtered candidates, not arbitrary neighbors. Having a legal war only opens the process; preparation, risk, cost, scoring and this final draw still matter.
captions.V3-11: Once war starts, armies need concrete destinations for siege, defense of the war objective, or approach to an enemy. The ordinary native objective path generates province candidates, pairs eligible armies with those provinces, and scores the pairs. A province suitable for one army need not suit another. The choice concerns an army going to a place, rather than a free-standing list of castle values.
captions.V3-12: One province can be found for several objective reasons. Its basic priority is not summed repeatedly: a higher priority replaces a lower one, and an equal priority keeps the existing record. Other modifiers may still apply. Being listed twice is different from receiving two copies of the basic score.
captions.V3-13: Objective blocks are supplied in order, but a later block can still matter when earlier provinces cannot cover the unassigned armies. Further work after an allocation round also has its own conditions. The process neither mixes every objective at once nor permanently stops merely because an early block found one province.
captions.V3-14: Army-province pairs are sorted by score, then checked against province use in this round, whether the army already has an assignment, and route validity when required. In a hypothetical list, A gets a castle at 90; B's 85-point plan for that same castle is skipped, so its 80-point alternative can be considered. Shared allocation changes what remains available to B.
captions.V3-15: A high-scoring pair can still fail a later path check. The native process checks its ordered candidates and marks passing arrangements; it does not solve a new global optimum after exploring every possible route. The work in this round is also bounded. The observed selection is a valid arrangement within that limited ordered search, not proof that every other route was worse.
captions.V3-16: Armies do not rebuild their whole objective list every instant. Target updates have a counter, an early recomputation route, and states that can defer the update. A target changing after several days does not by itself show that an enemy movement immediately caused the change. Trace the recomputation, changed candidates and allocation, then the written target and later action.
captions.V3-17: Different armies need not all run to the same valuable castle. Ordered and deduplicated province candidates are paired with armies, then constrained by this round's use, existing assignments, routes and final validity. Writing a target shows the selected destination; departure and the route taken belong to the next action stage.
captions.V3-18: The local approach metric is different from the declaration ratio of enemy strategic power to own power. In its normal return path, local estimated own power is divided by own power plus adjusted opposing power. With 100 on each side it is 0.5; with 200 versus 100 it is about 0.67. This share of a power total is not a measured probability of winning a battle.
captions.V3-19: The opposing input is not a raw sum of every nearby hostile flag. Native logic groups power by relationship and context, modifies hostile groups, uses a main group and half-weights other applicable groups, then applies further context adjustment. Visible soldier numbers alone cannot reproduce the metric. It serves the following action rules, separately from actual battle resolution.
captions.V3-20: The corresponding approach branch can use a normal strict threshold of 0.5 or a lower strict threshold of 0.4. A metric of 0.45 passes the lower gate but fails the normal one; exactly 0.5 still fails the normal strict comparison. The chosen gate changes which unfavorable power comparisons are allowed, but other objectives and route conditions still apply.
captions.V3-21: The lower setting is named 'desperate' in configuration, but that name is not its trigger rule. Selection first compares two power values at war-coordination level, then distinguishes war type and attacker or defender role. The ordinary defender path can also check army count, realm size and its own war score. A positive threshold on its own score is not equivalent to the opponent being ahead.
captions.V3-22: For a particular unfavorable adjacency before a target, a local metric below 0.625 can trigger a search for an alternative route with limited extra cost. If a suitable alternative exists, it is used; otherwise the current approach gate decides whether the original route can remain. Avoiding one entrance need not mean abandoning the target, and this local check does not promise safety along every future step.
captions.V3-23: To understand why an army sometimes approaches and sometimes detours, identify its adjusted local power metric, selected threshold, target and route checks. A soldier count or percentage alone skips those decisions. These are pre-contact choices; active retreat after a battle begins is a separate decision. The map becomes clearer when target, approach path and gate are read together.
captions.V3-24: Ordinary AI requests for support remember their previous state. If the army was not asking, the metric must be strictly below 0.66 to start. If it was already asking, it continues while still below 0.75. Thus two armies at 0.70 can have different request states because one previously asked for help and the other never crossed the starting threshold.
captions.V3-25: In a rule example with the prerequisites met, a unit starts asking at 0.65, keeps asking when it rises to 0.70, and stops at 0.76. Another unit that has never asked does not start at 0.70. The current number can be the same while prior state produces a different answer; the space between the thresholds prevents rapid switching near one line.
captions.V3-26: The two support thresholds do not apply to every flag unconditionally. In the traced ordinary producer, the requesting unit's parent AI stack needs more than one subunit; a singleton follows an earlier branch that clears its request. This counts internal AI organization, not the soldiers visible on a banner or nearby armies. First establish that the unit reached this decision at all.
captions.V3-27: A request does not automatically summon the nearest army. Cross-stack helper matching also checks whether a need remains: a quantized request value is compared with the requesting parent group's available power. If required power is 150, available power of 149 or 150 passes this check, while 151 continues to other candidates. The comparison describes the requester's remaining need, not a minimum size for the helper.
captions.V3-28: A request state, a helper assignment, and arrival in the same combat are separate changes. During a native update, parent groups are processed in stored order, so an earlier group may see a later group's previous request, while a later group may see a request just updated by an earlier one. Action submission follows. Two armies moving toward one place alone cannot prove a particular support match occurred.
captions.V3-29: An army can keep requesting help after it strengthens because it has not passed the stopping threshold. Whether help arrives also depends on matching, assignment and movement. These are ordinary AI-to-AI rules. Support for player armies has its own need, distance and arrival-time conditions; do not apply the same numbers to that separate path.
captions.V3-30: Winning a battle does not award a fixed amount of war score. In the traced single-battle calculation, hard losses inflicted on the loser are divided by a military quantity aggregated across the losing war participants, then the relevant cause's multiplier and per-battle cap apply. The numerator comes from this battle; the denominator is broader than the enemy army directly in front of you.
captions.V3-31: The denominator combines eight quantity categories. Levies and men-at-arms use their respective maximum-count measures, while special troops, knights and other categories have their own rules. It is neither the survivors of this battle nor a universal fully replenished army. It is a quantity total, not the strategic power weight used for declaration.
captions.V3-32: As a rule example, 1,000 hard losses against an aggregate of 10,000 are one tenth; with a hypothetical multiplier of 50 and no other cap, that contributes five. Against 20,000, the same losses contribute 2.5. The measure scales damage against this war's relevant size, and a real war uses the multiplier configured for its actual cause.
captions.V3-33: A battle result enters a single-battle record, then cumulative battle score by attacker or defender identity, with its cap. Overall war score also includes occupation, control of the war objective, important prisoners and other sources. A simultaneous change in the total panel cannot automatically be assigned entirely to one battle. Read the single entry, cumulative term and total in order, from the correct side's viewpoint.
captions.V3-34: To explain a modest score increase after a convincing win, check hard losses, which losing participants enter the denominator, the war's multiplier and caps, then cumulative and other total-score changes. A good battlefield result and a result sufficient to decide the whole war use different scales. Peace is another decision, with separate reasons to continue or stop.
captions.V3-35: Willingness to propose a white peace and willingness to accept one are separate calculations. The proactive inclination starts at zero and needs positive motivations; ordinary acceptance starts at minus thirty, then receives situational and character modifiers. One asks whether to offer terms now, the other whether to accept terms already received. An AI willing to accept need not send an offer itself.
captions.V3-36: In ordinary white-peace acceptance, the opponent's war score contributes to the recipient's calculation. For a defending recipient with other modifiers set to zero, attacker score 20 gives minus ten from the base of minus thirty; 30 gives zero; 31 gives plus one. Keep the attacker and defender identities fixed or the direction of this example becomes misleading.
captions.V3-37: On the verified legal, ordinary AI-recipient path without mediation, the acceptance score must be strictly greater than zero: zero still fails. War length, debt, other defensive wars, personality, peace-related abilities and hostages can change it. A later acceptance can therefore follow changed inputs; time alone is not a universal forced-peace switch.
captions.V3-38: The proactive side has a different ledger: war duration, its own score, debt, other defensive wars, personality and special circumstances can affect the inclination. Attacker and defender branches are not identical, and some branches set it to zero. Acceptance by the other party cannot supply the sender's motive. A natural offer requires tracing the sender's inputs and then the recipient's response.
captions.V3-39: Positive inclination still does not send an offer. The AI receives consideration opportunities, prepares legal recipients and interactions, then compares candidates. It converts inclination to an integer, subtracts a random integer from zero to ninety-nine, and requires the remainder to strictly beat a best value initially set to zero. No offer may win; the final send check remains. This is different from the declaration weighted draw.
captions.V3-40: Offers from an AI to a player face extra screening and zeroing rules. For example, when the AI defends and the attacking player's war score reaches ten, a relevant prefilter excludes that proactive offer. Making an AI lose more does not guarantee it will offer the player white peace. Its proactive decision and its response to a player's proposal remain distinct, and player-facing rules cannot simply be projected onto AI-to-AI wars.
captions.V3-41: After an offer is sent, its recipient must process the actual terms. For a real case, identify sender, recipient, conditions, response and whether the same war ended or continued. A rejection is also an informative outcome when its failed condition is known. A click or an 'would accept' hint alone does not establish that peace occurred.
captions.V3-42: A ruler can be willing to accept and still not propose peace because the two ledgers answer different questions. Acceptance evaluates received terms; proactive inclination, opportunity, random competition and the final send check determine whether an offer is made. One party may want to stop while the other refuses. No single universal 'war exhaustion' number is needed to explain both decisions.
captions.V3-43: War selection evaluates preparation, eligibility, power, cost and scored candidates. Army behavior assigns objectives and routes, compares local strength, and handles support requests and arrivals. Battle results become war-score contributions, while peace evaluates sender and recipient separately. These stages connect into a war, but they do not all reuse one 'chance of winning' measure.
captions.V3-44: Robert's two cards show what we can already read: an original target can resolve to a different effective defender, strategic power differs from soldier count, and ratios near 2.83 and 0.35 are not win probabilities. They show part of the native evaluation, not which war the AI ultimately chose. Its own preparation, scoring and selection would still be required.
captions.V3-45: When an AI hesitates, detours or does not offer peace, ask who is acting, which decision stage is active, which kind of power or score is compared, and what condition changed the result. A map screenshot cannot explain every cause by itself. The versioned decision diagrams, exact figures and sources are provided with the film so viewers can inspect a particular action more carefully.
